title: A second-order cone representable class of nonconvex quadratic programs
contribution: Extends RLT to continuous box-QPs via perspective inequalities and proves that QP(G) is SOC-representable when plus-loop nodes form a stable set, with a polynomial-size formulation under tree-decomposition conditions (C1)-(C3), generalizing Padberg's sparse Boolean-quadric-polytope results (read from arXiv v2).
problem_entry: Analogy with the Boolean quadric polytope: bounded treewidth gives polynomial LP extended formulations for sparse BQP, while the continuous QPn is open even for n = 3; the paper asks for a sparse-graph condition giving polynomial SOC formulations (pp. 2-5).
key_idea: Multiply z_ii >= z_i^2 by an RLT partition of unity and rewrite each term as a perspective of linearized RLT factors (Prop. 5, p. 11); with one plus loop this is exact (Thm. 1, p. 17), and decomposability glues pieces when plus-loop nodes are stable (Thm. 2, pp. 20-22) or a suitable tree decomposition exists (Thm. 3, p. 23).
assumptions: Box [0,1]^n, Q not PSD (p. 1); minus loops reduce to linear inequalities (Lemma 5, p. 8); plus-loop nodes stable (Thm. 2) and (C1) one plus loop per bag, (C2) width O(log|V|), (C3) spread O(log|V|) (p. 23); necessity of the stable-set assumption left open (p. 27).
proof_devices: Minkowski split S = S0 + S_inf for closedness (Lemma 2, p. 7)
Straszewicz plus explicit exposing linear function for extreme points (Lemma 3, pp. 7-8)
projection commutes with conv: added hyperedges give an extended formulation (Lemma 4, p. 8)
decomposability via a complete-hypergraph interface whose multilinear polytope is a simplex (Lemma 1 p. 6; Cor. 1 p. 9)
partition-of-unity RLT multiplication + closed perspective (Prop. 5, p. 11)
subadditivity of the perspective for hierarchy dominance (Prop. 6, p. 12)
explicit violated point with an LDL^T PSD certificate against SDP+MC+Tri (Prop. 7, pp. 13-14)
Balas disjunction on z_k in {0,1} faces + projection by substitution (Lemma 6), induction on n (Thm. 1, pp. 16-19)
clique completion of a plus-loop neighbourhood + induction on plus loops (Thm. 2, pp. 20-22)
bag consolidation and leaf peeling of a tree decomposition with a spread parameter (Lemmas 7-8, Thm. 3, pp. 23-25)
tailored tree decompositions for trees, chordless cycles and stars (Props. 8-10, pp. 25-26)
experiments: none (computational study named as future work, p. 27)
positioning: Continues Padberg, treewidth extended formulations, Sherali-Adams RLT and Del Pia-Khajavirad decomposability (pp. 4-10); prior RLT extensions are reframed as lacking extended-formulation guarantees (p. 10); sharpens Burer-Letchford n=3 inexactness (Cor. 2, p. 14) and shows the Anstreicher-Puges SOC relaxation is implied (Obs. 5, pp. 15-16).
writing: Contributions per section with a 'Roughly speaking' gloss (p. 5); worked examples after constructions (pp. 12, 20); proof-technique figure (p. 21); sparse precise hedging (p. 19); four concrete open questions (p. 27); small slip: 'Theorem 5' cited where Theorem 3 is meant (p. 27).
limits_future: Formulation may be exponential in general (p. 1); polynomial size needs O(log|V|) plus-loop degree/spread (pp. 22-23); complexity of checking (C1)-(C3), necessity of the stable-set condition, SOC extension-complexity lower bounds and solver integration are open (pp. 25, 27).

title: Aggregation of bilinear bipartite equality constraints and its application to structural model updating problem
contribution: Shows that aggregation closures give the hull of two bilinear bipartite equalities with at most three aggregations when n1 = n2 = 1, but may need infinitely many or fail entirely when n1 + n2 >= 3, and that one grid-searched aggregation per row pair still tightens relaxations and reduces final gaps in an FEM model-updating branch-and-bound (read from arXiv v1).
problem_entry: The one-row bilinear bipartite hull is known (SOC, disjunctive), so aggregate two rows into one and convexify; quadratic-aggregation results do not apply with variable bounds; FEM model updating as the application (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Study the aggregation closure (intersection over lambda of conv(S_lambda)) theoretically (Thms. 1-3, pp. 4-5), and computationally add the hull (polyhedral outer approximation) of one aggregation per row pair with weights chosen by distance-maximizing grid search (pp. 6-7, 11).
assumptions: S nonempty and the two rows independent (p. 4); variables scaled to [0,1] (pp. 1-2); computations use polyhedral approximations of the one-row hulls (p. 7); small dense random instances and simulated shear-frame FEM instances (pp. 8, 10); t = 2/5 aggregations chosen after preliminary experiments (p. 12).
proof_devices: aggregation to linearize one constraint plus affine change to (x - r)y = tau, then case analysis on point vs segment hulls (Thm. 1, pp. 14-15)
epsilon-perturbed aggregation whose hyperbola branch meets the line only on the opposite side; monotonicity/convexity of hyperbola branches and a mean-value argument (Obs. 1, pp. 14-20)
minimal example x*y1 = x*y2 = 0.5 with a perturbed point surviving any finite intersection (Thm. 2, pp. 22-23)
half-space families H+/- shrinking to y1 = y2 as theta -> 1 plus explicit two-point convex combinations (Thm. 2, pp. 23-26)
separating hyperplane via curve parametrization y(x) and maximizing g(x) (Thm. 3, pp. 26-27)
parameter-wise convex-combination certificates with points and weights rational in theta over six intervals (Thm. 3, pp. 27-30)
experiments: Julia/Gurobi/Ipopt, laptop; random (2,2),(3,3),(5,5) x10: one aggregation adds >10% / ~8% gap closure over one-row (p. 8); FEM 12-/16-story (9 each after exclusion): root improvements up to 6.82%/4.88% with grid search (p. 11); 1 h B&B vs BARON with shared OBBT bounds: average final gap 4.02/1.33/0.75% and 10.16/7.11/5.93% (BARON/one-row/aggregation), fewer nodes, losses on instance 3 reported (pp. 12-13); parallel grid time estimated, not measured (p. 9).
positioning: MILP aggregation lineage (Marchand-Wolsey, GMI as aggregation, Bodur et al., Dey-Molinaro) and surrogate relaxation lineage (Glover ... Mueller et al.) (pp. 2-3); quadratic-aggregation results reframed as inapplicable under bounds (p. 3); 9 of 21 references coauthored by Dey (pp. 30-31).
writing: Question-driven contributions (p. 3); all theorems with an example and proof idea up front, proofs at the back (pp. 3-5, 14-30); candid about difficulty and negative instances (pp. 5, 12); no future-work statement (pp. 13-14).
limits_future: Two rows only, one aggregation per pair, slow-down when adding all aggregations forced t = 2/5 (p. 12), parallel time estimated (p. 9); no future directions stated (pp. 13-14).

title: Water network design and operation optimization: Leveraging approximations
contribution: Proves that a coarse piecewise-linear MILP approximation of Hazen-Williams friction yields feasible, provably near-optimal produced-water network designs, and introduces a continuous-variable-diving heuristic (least-squares linearization with domain shrinkage) that improves three of nine best-known urban water network solutions.
problem_entry: Application-driven: Hazen-Williams q^1.85 nonconvexity defeats BARON on produced-water and urban networks; MILP approximations in the water literature lack guarantees (p. 2), while direct PWL is known to fail on urban networks (pp. 3, 14).
key_idea: (1) Four-interval PWL lambda-formulation with exact McCormick for binary x continuous products, plus repair propositions bounding the gap (Props. 3.1-3.3, pp. 8-14); (2) CVD: fit one least-squares line per nonlinearity, solve the MILP with a time limit, shrink each continuous domain around the solution by factor eta/2, and repeat (pp. 14-15).
assumptions: Prop. 3.2 needs chordless cycles and pressure slack of order |L||E|eps, claimed to hold on all instances without shown check (p. 11); Prop. 3.1 implicitly uses PWL overestimation of the convex q^1.85 (pp. 10-11); CVD needs bounded continuous variables, and Prop. 4.1 assumes unidimensional Lipschitz nonlinearities and feasible MILPs (pp. 14, 16).
proof_devices: repair construction: keep discrete decisions and flows, absorb the approximation error in valve/pump-head variables (Props. 3.1, 3.3, pp. 10, 13-14)
cycle-by-cycle pressure balancing; unidirectional cycles must contain a pump (Prop. 3.2, pp. 11-12)
pressure reassignment from sources with one global shift D (Prop. 3.2, pp. 12-13)
physical interpretation of cost bounds as pump operation scenarios (Remark, p. 14)

intermediate-value point where the least-squares fit equals f, plus a slope <= Lipschitz-constant lemma by rotation contradiction, giving a geometric-shrink iteration bound (Prop. 4.1 p. 16; Lemma 1 p. 27)
experiments: i7 laptop, Gurobi 12, BARON 25.2 (p. 16); PARETO case studies with stress and pump-cost scaling: PWL gaps 0.1-0.3% while BARON lacks good UBs in 3 h (Tables 3-4, pp. 17-18), gaps grow with pump cost up to 4.5% (Table 5); CVD on 9 MINLPLib urban instances beats best known on 3, worse on 4, fails New York without a two-piece variant, gaps to BARON LB up to 16.1% (Tables 6-7, pp. 19-20); PARETO Small 24-30% gap (Table 8); eta and time limits tuned on the same benchmark (pp. 21-22).
positioning: Criticizes MILP approximation work only for lacking guarantees (p. 2); accepts Bragalli et al. on PWL failure for urban networks (pp. 3, 14); places CVD between mesh refinement and integer diving (p. 4); cites Dey-Gupte pooling as the model (p. 2).
writing: Plain-language preface to each proposition and physical remarks on bounds (pp. 10-14); two-bullet contributions; one superlative ('consistently delivers near-optimal solutions for all ...', p. 4) not matched by Tables 6 and 8 (pp. 19-20).
limits_future: No limitations paragraph; implicit limits are the Prop. 3.2 assumptions, eta tuning and the New York failure (pp. 11, 19, 21); future: test CVD on other MINLPs with continuous nonlinearities (p. 23); no tightness examples for the bounds.

title: Distributed Linear Programming on GPU Clusters at Extreme Scale
contribution: SHARDLP keeps the LP matrix and primal-dual state partitioned across GPUs through every solver stage and adds support-aware communication; it solves 9 of 11 Google PDLP benchmark instances and independently validated LPs up to 13.6 billion variables and 40.8 billion nonzeros on 76 GPUs across 29 nodes.
problem_entry: Systems bottleneck: distributed PDHG products are not enough when other solver stages gather the problem on one node; the question is how to build a complete solver when neither matrix nor state fits on one node (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Persistent ownership of the D-PDLP R x C decomposition through input, scaling, restart, polishing, recovery and output, with no new PDHG variant (pp. 2-3, Table 7 p. 13), plus support-aware row reductions over only the GPUs holding nonzeros in that row (p. 5, App. D pp. 16-17).
assumptions: Prepartitioned shards with offline conversion excluded (pp. 3, 6); general presolve off, singleton-zero elimination only in RQ3 (p. 3); no infeasibility or unboundedness rays (p. 13); support-aware communication only for 1 x p column partitions with fixed support (pp. 6, 16).
proof_devices: exact-arithmetic equivalence of dense and support-aware executions by induction over participant epochs, with floating-point drift then measured (pp. 16-17)
logical scalar-hop ring communication model, explicitly not a byte or time prediction (eq. (8), p. 17)
experiments: PACE Phoenix cluster, H200/Blackwell/RTX 6000/V100 (App. A pp. 9-10); RQ1: 9/11 Google PDLP instances vs 8 published, TSP-Gaia-100M in 593 s solver time on 8 H200 vs published 21.06 h CPU, framed as coverage not controlled speed (Table 1 p. 4; p. 15); RQ2: up to 13.604B variables and 40.807B nonzeros, 76 GPUs / 29 nodes (Table 2 p. 5); RQ3: fixed-work loop 0.95x on 4 GPUs, support-aware 1.27x-1.52x on Design Match, 1.02x on QAP-WIL (pp. 5-6); nine-criterion independent original-space checker at 1e-6, uncheckable run not counted (pp. 13-15, 18).
positioning: Builds on PDHG/PDLP, cuPDLPx and D-PDLP, saying where borrowing stops ('Up to this point, the decomposition is D-PDLP's', p. 3); disclaims a new generic collective (p. 17); scope appendix disclaims 'first multi-node' and matched-speedup claims (pp. 17-18).
writing: RQ-structured (p. 3); three-sentence contributions (p. 2); distilled conclusion of two bottlenecks (p. 6); dense, precise hedging on every measurement type (pp. 10, 15, 17).
limits_future: Explicit limitations: offline sharding and support-aware communication only for column partitions (p. 6); future: partitioning, distributed presolve/postsolve, QP/SDP, and use as a subroutine in very large discrete optimization (p. 6).
